title: Technical Report
description: The technical report: numerical methods, validation against MPB, and benchmarks.
text:
January 8, 2026
Blaze2D: A High-Performance Solver for Photonic Crystals
Introducing Blaze: the design, validation, and performance of a Rust-based 2D Maxwell solver.
Photonic band structure calculations commonly rely on the Plane Wave Expansion (PWE) method, and MIT Photonic Bands (MPB) has long served as a widely used reference implementation for it. MPB is trusted for its accuracy and is therefore a natural baseline for performance comparisons.
Blaze is a Rust solver using LOBPCG and mixed-precision arithmetic. This report presents historical measurements of band calculations. It separates observed timings and memory use from hypotheses about their causes.
These historical benchmarks use square and hexagonal lattice configurations from Joannopoulos and colleagues' 1997 paper. Unless otherwise specified, all data reflects the square lattice configuration at a resolution of 64, computing the lowest 8 bands with 20 k-points per segment between high-symmetry points. Series 4 and 5 record MPB tolerance 1e-7 and Blaze tolerance 1e-4. The archived web datasets do not consistently record hardware identifiers or solver revisions, which limits reproducibility and cross-release comparisons.
Single-Core Performance
The computational cost of PWE solvers is dominated by Fast Fourier Transforms (FFTs). In this plane-wave formulation, Transverse Electric (TE) modes are more expensive to solve than Transverse Magnetic (TM) modes, because each operator application requires six FFTs rather than two for TM.
In these recorded single-core workloads, the f64 and mixed-precision Blaze runs are faster than the MPB runs. The mixed-precision measurements give an average speed ratio of about 2.9×. This ratio depends on the geometry, numerical settings, and execution environment.
Multi-Core Performance
The benchmark compares MPB threading within individual solves with Blaze scheduling independent configurations. The cost of synchronization and data movement can limit scaling for small problems.
Blaze avoids this overhead by parallelizing entire jobs rather than individual operations, a strategy optimized for large-scale parameter sweeps.
The recorded 16-thread runs give an average speed ratio of 11.9×. Blaze f64 times are approximately 240–350 ms, while mixed-precision times are about 160 ms. These timings alone do not identify a unique hardware bottleneck.
All subsequent benchmarks for Blaze are performed in Mixed Precision mode, unless otherwise specified.
Memory Efficiency
The recorded process-memory measurements are approximately 190 MB for MPB over much of this sweep. Process memory includes runtime and library allocations, so this observation does not establish that MPB reserves a fixed solver workspace.
Blaze uses less measured peak memory in these runs. A smaller working set can reduce data movement, but cache residency requires direct profiling and cannot be inferred from the memory ratio alone.
For a square grid with side length N, field storage grows as N^2 per band. Eigensolver workspaces also depend on band count, precision, and retained outputs. Process-level measurements may conceal that growth over a limited range.
Both recorded process-memory curves remain nearly flat over the tested band-count range. This does not imply that storing more eigenvectors has no memory cost.
Memory Scaling Laws
The measured MPB-to-Blaze memory ratio is about 20× at the smallest grids and decreases as the grid grows. These finite-range measurements do not determine an asymptotic memory ratio.
Power-law fits over the recorded range give exponents 0.06 for MPB and 1.09 for Blaze. These are empirical fits to process-memory measurements, not asymptotic storage laws or proof of a particular allocation strategy.
Resolution and Geometry
The viewer below illustrates grid resolution and interface smoothing for a circle. Blaze implements analytic subpixel averaging motivated by established dielectric-interface methods. Its present rasterizer does not guarantee MPB overlap precedence. Choose resolution through convergence tests for the geometry and quantities of interest.
Accuracy Validation
The reduction in precision and memory footprint raises a direct question: do we gain speed at the cost accuracy? To answer this question, we compared the eigenfrequencies from Blaze against a high-precision MPB reference along the full \Gamma \to X \to M \to \Gamma path. In the plots below, the MPB bands are drawn as lines and the Blaze eigenvalues as markers.
The comparison computes 20 bands and displays the lowest 10. Frequencies are compared as sorted eigenvalue sets at each wavevector, avoiding sensitivity to band labels near crossings and the upper edge of the solved window. This historical plotting convention differs from the current API, which preserves the tracked path returned by the solver.
Deviation Analysis
The recorded median relative frequency difference from MPB is about 1 \times 10^{-4}. The maximum is approximately 4 \times 10^{-4} for TM and 3 \times 10^{-4} for TE. These discrepancies measure agreement between runs; they are not certified bounds on discretization error.
The f32 and f64 Blaze runs differ by a median of about 1 \times 10^{-7} and a maximum below 5 \times 10^{-5}. Storage precision therefore has a smaller effect than the observed MPB difference in this dataset. Prior mixed-precision eigensolver studies provide related context.
Parallel Scaling
The two solvers parallelize in different ways. MPB splits the work inside a single solve across threads, while Blaze runs many independent solves at the same time, one per thread, which suits the parameter sweeps it is built for. The charts sweep the thread count from 1 to 16 and measure throughput in solves per second, for a small problem (N = 16) and a large one (N = 128).
For the recorded N=16 problem, Blaze throughput increases from about 28 to 220 solves per second across 16 threads. MPB threaded throughput stays near 14 solves per second. Separate MPB processes scale better than its threaded mode in this experiment.
For N=128, Blaze throughput increases by about 3× across the thread-count sweep. This supports scheduling independent configurations for these workloads; it does not establish a general limit on MPB parallelism.
Scaling with Resolution
Resolution sets the overall cost: the number of plane waves grows as N^2 and the FFTs as N^2 \log N. The bar chart sweeps the grid from N = 16 to N = 192 and compares wall-clock time against MPB.
Blaze is faster at each sampled resolution in this dataset. At N=192, the recorded times are approximately 8.0 s versus 39 s for TM and 12 s versus 70 s for TE. MPB timings vary non-monotonically with some grid sizes. FFT factorization and planning are possible contributors, requiring separate profiling.
The log-log plot compares empirical trends over the sampled resolutions. Its fitted slopes should not be extrapolated beyond this range without further measurements.
Convergence and Iteration Count
Beyond the cost of the entire single iteration, the number of iterations needed to converge each k-point matters.
Mean iteration counts are approximately 4.5 for Blaze TM and 5.6 for Blaze TE, compared with 7.5 and 11.9 for MPB. The recorded tolerances are 1e-4 for Blaze and 1e-7 for MPB, so these are not equal-tolerance iteration comparisons. Both implementations use eigenvalue changes in their stopping criteria. MPB documents this convention explicitly. Fresh residuals must be checked separately.
Maximum recorded iteration counts are 39 for MPB TM and 85 for MPB TE, compared with 12 and 24 for Blaze. Their locations vary along the path. The measurements do not isolate whether preconditioning, subspace updates, or stopping settings cause the difference.
Dielectric Contrast
The dielectric-contrast sweep covers rod permittivities from \varepsilon=2 to 13. Blaze times vary little over these sampled configurations; MPB times vary more. This is an observation about the recorded sweep, not a guarantee of contrast-independent cost.
Scaling with Band Count
The band-count sweep requests 4 to 20 bands. Solve time increases for both solvers. The recorded 20-band TM times are 1.9 s for Blaze and 3.9 s for MPB. Workspace size still depends on band count even where the process-memory measurements appear flat.
Conclusion
The recorded experiments show lower Blaze wall-clock times and peak process memory for the tested configurations. The reported ratios are specific to those measurements and their numerical settings. A matched comparison of release 0.7 requires new runs with explicit solver revisions, hardware, retained outputs, and residual checks.
Blaze schedules independent configurations and uses mixed-precision storage with f64 critical reductions. These design choices support repeated crystal calculations and scientific data extraction.
Blaze exports projected operator and derivative data, including velocity matrices, effective masses, and formulation-specific geometric terms. MPB also exposes fields, eigenvectors, and group velocities. Blaze integrates parameter studies and projected extraction in one configuration and result contract.

title: API & TOML
description: One versioned calculation contract for Python, native tools, and the Workbench.
text:
API & TOML
A blaze2d/1 configuration describes a calculation independently of its runner.
Rust resolves defaults, validates geometry and numerical settings, and expands studies.
Python, the command line, and the Workbench consume the same normalized jobs.
A band calculation
The optional sections are [eigensolver], [dielectric], [results], and
[[sweeps]]. Choose task = "bands" with [bands], or task = "operators"
with [operators]. Supplying both task sections is an error. Unknown keys and
unsupported precision, geometry, material, or dimension requests also fail explicitly.
An empty object list is a valid homogeneous medium.
| Section | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| geometry | Direct lattice, background permittivity, and named objects |
| grid | Scalar resolution or an explicit [nx, ny] |
| bands / operators | Calculation, band window, and sampling |
| sweeps | Ordered, typed parameter axes |
| eigensolver | Precision, stopping tolerance, iteration limit, and block size |
| dielectric | Sampling, smoothing, mesh size, and interface tolerance |
| results | Retention of optional large datasets |
Object names are unique. Use geometry.objects.rod.radius as a sweep target.
A lattice uses either a preset with lengths, or type = "custom" with explicit
vectors. Rectangular lattices require b; oblique lattices also require angle_deg.
The current release supports two-dimensional circles and positive scalar permittivity.
Defaults and coordinates
Defaults are grid 32 × 32, f64, eight bands, and analytic dielectric smoothing
with mesh size 3 and interface tolerance 1e-6. Eigenvector retention is off.
Band calculations use 200 iterations. Operators use 1e-8 and 300 iterations,
starting at band 0 with four retained and eight upper remote bands.
Native f64 band calculations stop when every requested band's relative residual
‖Au − λBu‖/(‖Au‖ + |λ|‖Bu‖) is at most residual_tolerance (1e-7), confirmed with
fresh operator applications. Operator calculations, an explicit tolerance (also as
a sweep target), f32 storage, or the browser select the relative eigenvalue
change rule instead (default 1e-6 for bands, 1e-8 for operators); f32 storage
has a grid-dependent residual floor and supports only that rule. Set stopping = "residual" or
"eigenvalue_change" to choose explicitly. Normalized configurations keep "auto",
so an exported configuration resolves again when edited. Fresh operator
residuals and orthogonality defects are reported in either case. Set
operators.fail_on_residual to enforce a normalized residual acceptance threshold.
Without that gate, a completed calculation may still contain inaccurate remote eigenvectors.
Band results report fresh residuals and B-orthogonality without rotating the tracked fields.
Operator results include the existing final Rayleigh-Ritz refinement.
Experimental solver settings live under [eigensolver] and [eigensolver.preconditioner]
and can be swept. history chooses the LOBPCG search block ("ritz", the next Ritz
vectors; "conjugate", Knyazev's implicit directions; "none"). The preconditioner
kind is "auto" (Fourier diagonal for TM, transverse projection for TE),
"diagonal", "transverse" or "none". Its shift rule is "continuous" by
default (shift_fraction, default 0, times the smallest |k+G|², in |k+G|² units for
both kinds, so it vanishes at Γ); "legacy" uses shift_fraction (default 0.5) times
the smallest |k+G|² above 1e-6 (scaled by the effective permittivity in the Fourier
diagonal), and "band_window" and "fixed" (shift_value) remain.
transverse_weight = "tensor" (the default) weights the transverse projection with the
inverse of the smoothed ε⁻¹ tensors the operator uses; "scalar" uses ε. coarse_modes
adds an additive two-level correction on the lowest plane waves, with a Galerkin matrix
assembled exactly from the material's Fourier coefficients and shifted by coarse_shift. profile weights the
preconditioner T as W^½ T W^½, where W multiplies each plane wave by exp τ(s) with
s = |k+G|²/|b_min|² (b_min the shortest reciprocal lattice vector) and τ is piecewise linear
in ln s through knots at s = 1/16, 1/4, …, 1024 and constant outside them. It takes eight
knot values, "none", or "auto" (the default): a built-in profile, fitted to band runs,
for the TE transverse projection with the continuous shift at zero, the tensor weight and
no coarse correction, and none otherwise. Every profile keeps the preconditioner Hermitian positive definite and
symmetric, and zeros reproduce it. On the preconditioner study matrix the defaults needed
18% (TE) and 10% (TM) fewer FFTs in total than shift = "legacy" with
transverse_weight = "scalar" and profile = "none", and more on no diagram. Results report the
resolved settings per k point in metadata.preconditioner and solver work counters
in metadata.work.
For an explicit band acceptance contract, add:
[bands.accuracy]
max_relative_residual = 1e-5
max_absolute_residual = 1e-7
max_orthogonality_defect = 1e-8
Every returned mode must pass the relative or absolute residual limit, the
whole block must pass B-orthogonality, and every requested point must meet the
stopping criterion. The absolute branch remains meaningful at zero or near-zero
Gamma modes. Limits must be finite and positive; omitted limits take the values
above. Omitting the entire section preserves the previous reporting-only behavior.
The gate covers ordinary solves, reuse, final fallbacks, metric support and
external sampled inputs. It never silently tightens the stopping tolerance.
Rejected ordinary jobs preserve their computed arrays in partial_result and
follow the runner's error policy. An empty or invalid certificate cannot pass.
This is a backward-error check on the selected finite pencil. Metric-support
acceptance uses its projected pencil; material/grid convergence, continuum
accuracy and complete low-band coverage remain separate questions.
absolute_residuals contains \|Au-\lambda Bu\|/\|u\|. Use it near Gamma,
where a small denominator can make normalized residuals misleading. Both arrays
follow the returned band order; their conventions and units are recorded in metadata.
Lattice vectors and circle radii share one reference length.
Object centers and registry displacements use direct fractional coordinates.
Reciprocal fractional coordinates use k = 2\pi A^{-T}q.
Cartesian wavevectors are angular wavevectors in inverse reference-length units.
Frequencies are \sqrt{\lambda}/(2\pi), in units of c per reference length.
Operator derivatives keep their recorded differentiation basis. Changing the carrier coordinate representation does not change that basis.
A band path is a preset, vertices with intervals_per_segment, or already sampled
points. These forms cannot be combined. A path with S segments and N intervals
per segment has SN+1 samples. Distances use the reciprocal Cartesian metric.
Labels retain their exact sample indices. Certified identical-point reuse eliminates
the solve at a closing Gamma point; the automatic policy selects it whenever the path
repeats a point and max_cache_bytes is positive.
Symmetry and execution reports
Without mechanism keys, policy resolves to "auto". Writing any mechanism key,
even with its default value, selects "manual"; memory limits and plane_group are
not mechanisms. External dielectric input always runs manually. residual-pt-v1
considers PT on native f64 equal square/triangular FFT grids 16–128 with 8–16 bands
under residual stopping between 1e-8 and 1e-6, for objects that are symmetric
under inversion about the cell origin. Under eigenvalue-change stopping it keeps the
earlier envelope (grids 31–65, tolerance at most 1e-13), where triangular metric
support also requires the measured cutoff range described in Symmetries.
Elsewhere the complex path is used. Every PT and repeated-point result still requires
its own certificate.
Auto never changes material sampling, Fourier support or precision. Native PT
profitability is not assumed in the browser. Requested and resolved settings,
retained methods, coordinate blocks, reused points, all attempted iterations
and fallback reasons appear in metadata.execution. The concise text field
also appears in the Workbench and on CLI stderr; --quiet suppresses the CLI
summary. Standard output remains machine-readable JSON. Python prints nothing
automatically; use print(blaze.execution_summary(result_or_study)).
| Maturity | Options and intended use |
|---|---|
| Recommended within the measured envelope | Native f64 auto, final accuracy acceptance, ordinary complex fallback |
| Advanced, explicitly qualified | Manual PT/Fourier choices, k-star transport, sectors, partner reconstruction, bounded geometry continuation and coarse starts |
| Explicit discretization choice | Metric Fourier support and Voronoi material averages; compare to the same pencil before claiming acceleration |
| Experimental Rust APIs | Geometry-response prediction, precision changes, shared iteration engine and specialized scheduling; no general speed recommendation |
Some advanced combinations cost more than the ordinary solve. The
replacement notes retain those negative results.
Parameter studies
[[sweeps]]
name = "radius"
target = "geometry.objects.rod.radius"
linspace = { start = 0.16, stop = 0.24, count = 5 }

[[sweeps]]
name = "polarization"
target = "polarization"
values = ["TM", "TE"]
Use values or linspace, with inclusive endpoints and a count. Descending
interpolation is valid. The first axis is outermost and the last varies fastest.
Each combination starts from the immutable base configuration. Results preserve
axis values, job indices, and integer multi-indices.
Thread counts, error policy, and output paths are runner options. The default
failure policy stops the study while retaining completed jobs. Native scheduling
parallelizes independent configurations with bounded result delivery.
Operators, registry studies, and stencils
band_lo is zero-based. The solved window includes lower bands, retained bands,
and upper remote bands. Arrays record the actual band-index sets.
Supported quantity groups are velocity, mass_tensor, r_derivatives,
born_huang, slow_coefficient, exact_tm, and overlap, subject to the
polarization and reference requirements of the current formulation. Dependency
quantities may be computed automatically; computed and retained quantities are recorded.
[operators.registry]
object = "hole"
points = [[0.0, 0.0], [0.25, 0.25]]
fd_step = 0.001

[operators.k_stencil]
points_per_axis = 3
half_width = 0.02
Generic sweep axes are outermost, registry points follow, and a stencil runs at
each configuration. Registry translations start from the base model and wrap
periodically. Independent registry points retain independent gauges.
K-stencils solve the center first and transport along the existing adjacent walk.
Returned sample order is recorded separately. A one-point stencil is valid.
Overlap extraction needs a reference source; stencil neighbors use internal references.
Python
Config.from_file, .from_toml, and .from_dict validate through Rust.
config.to_dict() and .to_toml() expose normalized settings.
blaze.solve(config) runs exactly one calculation and returns a dictionary.
blaze.run(config, threads=4) returns results, errors, and run statistics.
blaze.stream(config) yields completed records incrementally.
blaze.build_info() and .capabilities() report the installed backend.
blaze.execution_summary(result_or_study) reports requested and actual execution.
Simple band calculations also accept scalar convenience arguments to blaze.solve.
Numerical lists do not implicitly create sweeps. Plotting and terminal output are optional extras.
| Dataset | NumPy shape |
| --- | --- |
| frequencies | (k_point, band) |
| Operator eigenvalues | (solved_band,) |
| Operator eigenvectors | (solved_band, ny, nx) |
| velocity_matrices | (direction, retained_band, solved_band) |
| w_matrices, mass_tensor_inv | (direction, direction, retained_band, retained_band) |
| Registry and metric derivatives | (direction, retained_band, solved_band) |
Arrays use C order, with flattened grid index iy * nx + ix. Complex output is
NumPy complex128, including when solver storage uses f32. Metadata records
storage and accumulation precision, coordinates, convergence, provenance, and shapes.
Raw eigenvectors from different gauges should be compared through subspace invariants.
For mode visualization, blaze.align_modes(result, reference_fields,
reference_frequencies, bands=[0, 1, 2], weights=epsilon) returns separate
fields, a unitary transform and cluster diagnostics. Supply one reference
k point on the same physical cell/grid and in the same coordinate convention;
frequencies use Blaze's units. bands contains source indices, even when path
tracking has reordered them. TE defaults to Euclidean weights; TM requires
positive physical mass/quadrature weights. Both spectra must contain a separated
upper guard band beyond each selected complete cluster. The helper rejects
split clusters, incompatible spans and nonorthogonal frames. It preserves
pointwise summed cluster intensity and leaves the solve gauge and certificates
unchanged. Its returned visualization frame needs fresh certification before
numerical reuse; a nearly degenerate rotation is not automatically a set of
exact eigenpairs.
eigenvalue_atol and eigenvalue_rtol bound each cluster's squared-frequency
spread in both spectra. An independently computed reference may need an explicit
larger tolerance for numerical splitting; the helper never infers that permission
from a similar-looking image.
blaze.OperatorDataExtractor retains native reference-field, external dielectric,
and checkpoint workflows. Its methods take the shared configuration. External
fields use a complete solved-band block; reference overlaps select the retained window.
External dielectric input declares dielectric.source = "external", an empty
object list, and one sampled band point. These inputs are unavailable in the browser.
This sampled-point entry point supports the ordinary spatial solve and final
accuracy acceptance; nondefault symmetry options are rejected explicitly.
Command line and export
blaze2d config validate calculation.toml
blaze2d config normalize calculation.toml
blaze2d config describe
blaze2d run calculation.toml -o results.npz
Both the Python entry point and native CLI share the contract. Use blaze.save
and blaze.load for JSON or NPZ. write_ndjson and read_ndjson support streams.
Exports include explicit array descriptors and complex encoding. NPZ includes a
UTF-8 metadata manifest and loads without pickle. Checkpoint resumption validates
the normalized configuration and build before skipping completed jobs.

text:
Blaze2D: A Rust Maxwell solver for photonic crystals
Blaze computes band structures, configuration studies, and projected
operators for 2D periodic dielectrics. Built for fast, large-scale parameter
sweeps, it exposes operator data unavailable in conventional solvers such as MPB.
Created for a master’s thesis in theoretical physics at TU Dortmund
University on photonic moiré crystals, Blaze remains actively
developed. Its methods, measurements, and reasoning are documented
here.
Use Blaze through Python
(pip install blaze2d), the command line, or this website’s interactive
browser tool, which requires no installation.
New to photonic band structures? Start with the introduction.
What this website answers

title: Installation
description: Install the Python package and run your first calculation.
text:
Installation
Install Blaze2D with Python 3.10 or later:
python -m pip install blaze2d
Release wheels cover Linux x86_64 (glibc 2.17+), macOS 11+ on x86_64 and arm64, and Windows 10+ on x86_64. NumPy is required. Plotting and terminal progress are optional: python -m pip install 'blaze2d[plot,progress]'.
A first calculation
import blaze

result = blaze.solve(resolution=32, n_bands=8)
print(result["frequencies"].shape)  # (k_point, band)
The default model is a square lattice with one dielectric rod. Results are dictionaries with named NumPy arrays and numerical metadata. Use Examples to explore other models, or open the Workbench to configure a calculation in the browser.
A reproducible study
Download a TOML example or export a configuration from the Workbench:
blaze2d config validate calculation.toml
blaze2d run calculation.toml --output results.npz
The API & TOML reference describes normalization, sweeps, and operator extraction.
Build from source
Install Rust 1.91.1, then clone the repository:
git clone https://github.com/RnLe/blaze2d.git
cd blaze2d
python -m pip install ./crates/python
cargo build --release -p blaze2d-cli
The native CLI is written to target/release/blaze2d. To run the scientific and contract tests:
cargo test -p blaze2d-core -p blaze2d-interface -p blaze2d-runner
python -m pytest crates/python/tests
Benchmarks
The technical report describes the recorded experiments. The repository's benchmarks/ directory contains their data and scripts. Historical timings apply to the stated hardware, configuration, and solver revision; they are not performance guarantees for every model or release.

headings.text: How do I read a band diagram?
How does Blaze solve the equation?
What can operator data tell us?

text:
Introduction
Blaze2D computes photonic bands and projected Maxwell operators for two-dimensional periodic dielectric structures. It is written in Rust and available through Python, TOML files, a native command, and the browser Workbench.
This page builds the physical picture those calculations rest on: what makes a crystal photonic, how a repeating structure is described, and what a band structure actually reports.
What makes a crystal photonic?
A photonic crystal is a material whose dielectric permittivity repeats in space.
Alternating glass and air layers are a simple example. Light scattered by the repeated
interfaces interferes, allowing some waves to travel through the structure while
excluding others. The pattern and dielectric contrast determine that response.
To describe a repeating pattern, separate its lattice from its basis. The lattice
specifies the translations: integer steps along two primitive vectors,
\mathbf{a}_1 and \mathbf{a}_2. The basis is the arrangement of objects repeated
at each lattice point. There are five Bravais lattice types in two dimensions.
Place a dielectric rod at every point, or an air hole in a uniform dielectric, and
the lattice becomes a photonic crystal. A basis can also contain several objects.
For example, a honeycomb pattern uses a triangular lattice with two sites per cell.
The lattice sets the translations; the basis, object sizes, and materials set the
permittivity within each cell.
Why does light form bands?
The geometry enters Maxwell's equations through the relative permittivity
\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}). For a lossless, nonmagnetic material without frequency
dispersion, the magnetic field obeys the photonic master equation:
Here \mathbf{H} is a mode's magnetic field, \omega its angular frequency, and c
the speed of light in vacuum. This is an eigenvalue problem: find the field patterns
whose shape is unchanged by the operator on the left. The scale factor is the
eigenvalue \omega^2/c^2.
If you know electronic band theory, the connection is direct. A periodic potential
acts on an electron's wavefunction in the Schrödinger equation. A periodic
permittivity acts on an electromagnetic field in Maxwell's equations. Both admit
Bloch waves and bands, although the fields, operators, and physical observables differ.
Periodicity lets us write each mode as a plane wave multiplied by a function that
repeats in every cell:
The Bloch wavevector \mathbf{k} sets the phase change from cell to cell.
For each \mathbf{k}, the master equation gives a sequence of allowed frequencies.
Following the nth frequency as \mathbf{k} changes gives a band,
\omega_n(\mathbf{k}).
How do I read a band diagram?
A band diagram plots those frequencies along a path through the Brillouin zone,
the region of distinct Bloch wavevectors. Labels such as \Gamma, X, M, and K
mark points of lattice symmetry. The horizontal axis is a path in wavevector space,
not a position inside the crystal.
Each curve is one allowed mode frequency. The vertical axis uses
\omega a/(2\pi c)=a/\lambda_0, where a is the lattice constant and \lambda_0
the vacuum wavelength. This normalization makes the diagram independent of the
overall scale of a nondispersive crystal.
The blue curves are TM modes, with the electric field along the invariant
direction. Orange curves are TE modes, with the magnetic field in that direction.
On the left, the shaded interval excludes TM modes but still contains TE modes.
On the right, the shaded interval is shared by both polarizations. A complete
band gap requires an absence of modes throughout the Brillouin zone, so checking
only the plotted path is not sufficient to establish it.
Band slopes also carry information: \nabla_{\mathbf{k}}\omega_n gives the group
velocity. A flatter band means slower propagation in the corresponding direction.
These frequencies and field patterns are the basic results returned by a band solver.
How does Blaze solve the equation?
MPB and Blaze use a plane-wave expansion
(PWE). Once the Bloch phase is separated out, the remaining field is periodic.
It can therefore be represented by a finite set of Fourier components, labelled
by reciprocal lattice vectors \mathbf{G}:
For Blaze's 2D scalar problems, u is the periodic part of H_z for TE or E_z for TM.
The coefficients \mathbf{c}_n are the unknowns. A represents the differential
operator; B is the identity for TE and the dielectric weight for TM.
An iterative eigensolver finds the requested bands at each wavevector. Increasing
the grid resolution adds Fourier components, and convergence checks show whether
the chosen resolution is sufficient.
01Define the cellLattice, objects, permittivity
02Solve at each kPeriodic fields and frequencies
03Trace the bandsDispersion, gaps, mode profiles
Blaze currently supports two-dimensional circles and positive scalar dielectric
materials. This covers rods, holes, and multi-object bases on any 2D Bravais lattice.
Its rods and holes extend uniformly along the third direction.
Why calculate many different crystals?
One band diagram answers a question about one configuration. Designing a crystal
or building a model often requires a parameter study: repeat the calculation
while changing the geometry or material.
Rod or hole radiusWhere does a gap open or close?
Positions in the basisHow do alignment and symmetry change the bands?
Dielectric constantHow does material contrast shift the frequencies?
In many short solves, geometry setup can become a substantial repeated cost.
MPB's geometry initialization
samples and averages the dielectric near interfaces.
Blaze targets this overhead with specialized circle geometry and analytic boundary
area fractions, and schedules independent configurations across CPU cores. Its
ordered sweeps retain the parameter values alongside each result.
The technical report compares complete calculation times against MPB
under stated settings. Those timings include both setup and solving; the benefit
depends on the geometry, resolution, and number of requested bands.
What can operator data tell us?
A band diagram shows where the modes lie. It does not, by itself, tell us how two
modes couple when a structure changes. That requires matrix elements of the
operator and its derivatives between the computed fields.
MPB already exposes frequencies, electromagnetic fields, raw eigenvectors, and
group velocities through its Python interface.
It does not provide Blaze's prepared collection of projected derivative matrices
and associated coordinate and phase-convention metadata. Deriving these from MPB
output requires an additional extraction workflow.
Both solvers use matrix-free operator application: they evaluate A\mathbf{v}
for a trial field without storing the full matrix A. Fourier transforms connect
spatial derivatives to material multiplication. This saves memory, and it still
allows small projected matrices to be computed by applying an operator to selected
fields and taking their inner products.
For example, let L be the periodic TE operator. A parameter p such as a wavevector
component or an object's displacement gives the derivative matrix
Here the fields are normalized within the unit cell. Away from degeneracies,
diagonal entries describe the first-order change in an eigenvalue; off-diagonal
entries describe mixing between different modes. Near a degeneracy, the coupled
bands must be treated together.
| Data available in Blaze | Physical use |
| --- | --- |
| Wavevector derivatives and curvature matrices | Propagation, coupling between bands, and effective masses understood as band curvature |
| Derivatives with respect to object displacement | Perturbations caused by changing the relative alignment of objects in a cell |
| Cross-band matrix elements and overlaps between sampled states | Reduced models that retain selected bands and track changes in their basis |
For TM, the dielectric weight and its derivatives must also be included; Blaze
records those separately. The operator reference
specifies the available quantities and conventions.
This is the connection to the master's thesis. A twisted photonic crystal
can be described through many locally periodic crystals whose alignment changes
slowly in space. Their bands supply the local frequencies. Their projected operator
data supply coefficients for an effective model of the slow variation. Blaze was
built to make both parts of that calculation practical.
To calculate a first band diagram, open an example or follow the
installation guide.

title: Optimization & Roadmap
description: A staged roadmap for Blaze: a research foundation, broader and faster 2D calculations, then GPU execution, 3D crystals, and slabs.
text:
Actively developed
Optimization & Roadmap
This page maps the development of Blaze into stages, grouping related modules so that later work can build on a mature foundation. Each module is marked , , or .
Blaze was built specifically for a master's thesis, with a narrower
application than established reference solvers: two-dimensional photonic crystals,
repeated parameter studies, and projected Maxwell operators. It remains actively
developed, with broader capabilities and further optimization as the next
research priorities.
MPB remains Blaze's strongest reference and principal validation target.
Adopting and optimizing MPB's capabilities is a natural direction,
while retaining Blaze's emphasis on sweeps and operator data.
Stage 1: Research foundation
Establish a reliable research core. Exact symmetry workflows and their reference
controls are implemented; geometry continuation remains an experimental policy.
2D research core
Blaze's research core computes TE and TM bands for circular inclusions in positive
scalar dielectrics, runs parameter sweeps, and projects Maxwell operators. Native and browser
execution share a configuration format. MPB comparisons and convergence metadata
provide the baseline for further work.
Symmetries
Exact affine actions qualify the sampled material, tensor and finite Maxwell
pencil before reuse or reduction. Blaze implements equivalent-wavevector reuse,
ordinary/projective sectors, qualified PT real coordinates and selected reduced
kernels. A measured automatic policy selects native PT and repeated-point reuse;
triangular support and Voronoi material qualification have separate convergence
evidence. Read the Symmetries theory and
replacement notes with benchmarks for the supported
combinations, measured gains and retained regressions.
Configuration warm starts
Native/Python sweeps and serial browser calculations now carry certified mode
information across geometries and complete k paths. Worker caches are bounded;
target-mass seed preparation and ordinary-solve fallback preserve numerical
checks and original job order. Full-path and first-point policies are explicit:
matched public sweeps did not justify enabling them automatically. The
public workflow measurements
include both gains and regressions. Rust research APIs also expose snapshot
enrichment and geometry-response predictors. MPB's standard run resets fields,
although explicit reuse is possible. Published methods for
tracking Maxwell modes as geometry changes provide related context.
Warm starts already matter within a single crystal's k-space workflow. Cross-geometry reuse needs its own complete-sweep evidence: preparation and failed attempts can outweigh fewer final iterations.
Theory and benchmarks
Keep this website up-to-date with the theory, implementation reasoning, and reproducible
measurements. Profile setup, FFTs, orthogonalization, allocations, and memory. Compare
total runtime at equal accuracy, with configurations, hardware, and tolerances
reported alongside the results.
Stage 2: Generalize and optimize 2D
Fully generalize 2D geometry, improve solving, and support MPB workflows.
MPB remains the reference for the extended capabilities.
General geometry
Add polygons, composite shapes, and imported dielectric grids, with clear overlap
rules and accurate material-interface sampling. Initially retain positive scalar
permittivity. Tensor materials, loss, and dispersion would need separate extensions
to the physical formulation.
Solver optimization
Tune the existing block eigensolver, preconditioning, memory layout, and precision
choices. Then add calculations near a chosen frequency, a capability MPB already
offers. Evaluate alternative algorithms against difficult or clustered bands,
with the same residual accuracy and requested band coverage.
Gradients and inverse design
Extend operator workflows with geometry and material derivatives. Minkov and
colleagues demonstrated photonic-crystal inverse design through automatic
differentiation. Blaze needs derivatives consistent with its
discrete operators, including careful treatment of interfaces and degenerate modes.
MPB compatibility
Begin with equivalent examples, geometry conversion, and a scoped Python adapter.
Match units, field normalization, metadata, and required exports such as HDF5.
Broader Python or Scheme compatibility can follow as tested workflows expand.
Stage 3: GPU, 3D, and slabs
Build on the optimized 2D core to make large parameter studies more practical and
study structures beyond the 2D TE/TM model. GPU parallelism targets faster band
calculations, while 3D and slab models add polarization coupling and vertical
confinement.
GPU execution
Keep FFTs, material operations, preconditioning, and block algebra on the device
throughout a solve. Jin and Xie report over 40× average acceleration for their
3D finite-difference solver using CuPy on an RTX 4090 D against a NumPy CPU
implementation. Blaze's plane-wave solver needs its own measurements.
Higher throughput could make large sweeps and training datasets more affordable. For example, Feng's neural waveguide design study trains on MPB band diagrams across varying geometries. Faster dataset generation is a useful application of a GPU backend.
Full 3D Maxwell
Extend to lossless periodic 3D crystals with vector fields, 3D FFTs, and material
sampling. The scalar TE/TM split no longer applies: enforce transverse fields and
handle the curl operator's null space, with a larger memory budget.
Photonic slabs
Guided-mode expansion uses the modes of an unpatterned waveguide as a reduced basis
for efficient slab band calculations, combining periodicity in the plane with vertical
confinement. Legume implements this for photonic crystal slabs.
A similar extension could expose slab bands, fields, and radiative losses, within
the method's basis and perturbative radiation approximations.
Ideas and contributions are warmly welcome, whether a useful test case, a numerical method, or a clearer explanation. Join the project on GitHub.
