title: Symmetries
description: Exact crystal actions, qualified Bloch reuse, sector coverage, and real or reduced coordinates in Blaze's finite Maxwell problems.

headings.text: The Maxwell pencil is the contract
Storage reduction and reduced operator work

text:
Symmetries
A symmetry can save an entire solve, reduce the work within a solve, or reduce
stored data. These are different mechanisms. Blaze checks each against the
material and the finite Maxwell problem actually being solved. A lattice
label alone does not authorize a reduction.
The implementation covers exact affine operations for all 17 plane groups,
equivalent-wavevector reuse, ordinary and projective sectors, qualified PT real
coordinates, and selected reduced kernels. Each mechanism has an unrestricted
control and explicit eligibility checks. Some combinations remain unsupported;
some correct reductions cost more than they save. The
replacement notes record those limits and the measurements.
The Maxwell pencil is the contract
After separating the Bloch phase, Blaze solves a finite generalized eigenproblem
For TM, u represents the periodic part of E_z, A_{\mathbf{k}} is the
Bloch Laplacian and B is the sampled dielectric weight. For TE, u represents
H_z, B=I, and the operator contains the sampled inverse dielectric tensor
between Bloch derivatives. Smoothing can produce such a tensor even when the
physical dielectric is scalar. Reported normalized frequencies also include
Blaze's length and 2\pi conventions.
Let T_g map coefficients at \mathbf{k} to coefficients at \mathbf{k}'.
A usable unitary symmetry must preserve both forms of the pencil:
For an antiunitary action, the corresponding covariance identities also
include complex conjugation.
Blaze checks the lattice metric, scalar material, inverse tensor, sample mapping,
retained Fourier support and operator action. A point permutation on a periodic
array is insufficient: wrapping a Fourier index can change its derivative,
especially at an even grid's Nyquist boundary. Qualification is specific to the
grid, material, wavevector and representation.
Affine closure and lattice carries are exact. Material/operator covariance and
field accuracy are numerical checks with explicit tolerances and rejection
reasons.
Coordinates, translations and field signs
Write the direct lattice vectors as the columns of L and use fractional
coordinates \boldsymbol\xi and \boldsymbol\kappa:
An affine operation is g=(W,\boldsymbol\tau), acting as
\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto W\boldsymbol\xi+\boldsymbol\tau.
W is an integer lattice automorphism; translations and origin shifts use exact
rational arithmetic. Its Cartesian action is R=LWL^{-1}. A point symmetry
satisfies W^T L^T L W=L^T L. This distinction between fractional and Cartesian
coordinates matters on oblique and hexagonal cells.
Composition retains the integer lattice translation left by the chosen
representatives:
The carry \boldsymbol\ell contributes a Bloch phase; discarding it changes the
representation. For a unitary operation, let \mathbf{m}_g fold the transformed
wavevector into the chosen reciprocal cell. A Fourier coefficient transforms as
For in-plane operations, D(R)=1 for TM's polar E_z, while
D(R)=\det R for TE's axial H_z. Thus a physical reflection label for TE
differs from the label obtained by treating H_z as an ordinary scalar.
Antiunitary actions additionally conjugate the coefficients and reverse the
wavevector before folding. The physical time-reversal sign is also retained:
E_z is even and H_z is odd under time reversal.
The exact group catalogue includes centered settings in primitive coordinates.
It does not imply that every group acts on every rectangular FFT support. In
particular, a valid hexagonal rotation need not preserve a rectangular set of
Fourier modes. Unsupported actions are rejected rather than aliased into place.
| Conventional setting | Plane groups in the catalogue |
|---|---|
| General / oblique | p1, p2 |
| Primitive rectangular | pm, pg, pmm, pmg, pgg |
| Centered rectangular | cm, cmm |
| Square | p4, p4m, p4g |
| Hexagonal | p3, p3m1, p31m, p6, p6m |
These are conventional settings, not an inference from the lattice alone. A
motif on a square or hexagonal lattice can retain only a smaller group.
Reuse between wavevectors
The star of a wavevector contains points related by qualified crystal
operations. Blaze can solve one representative and reconstruct the requested
fields at the others. Identical requests have an even simpler reuse path.
For real reciprocal materials, qualified time reversal can provide additional
equivalences, but only orbits not already covered by unitary operations count as
extra savings.
Reuse preserves requested point order, weights, complex fields and numerical
certificates. An optional traversal changes execution order to improve
continuation, then restores the user's order. These gains have different causes:
star reuse eliminates solves; traversal attempts to make the remaining solves
easier. A sparse path with no equivalent points cannot obtain the former gain.
Cache entries carry the operator, support and representation identity. Only
matching finite operators qualify for exact reuse. Fields from nearby, different
problems may instead become
seeds, after rank extraction and Ritz preparation in the new problem's mass
metric. Several nonzero projected columns can still span only one direction.
Sectors and complete band coverage
The little group preserves a fixed wavevector modulo reciprocal translations.
Its representations split the mode space into invariant sectors. Matrix units
can select individual rows of a multidimensional representation:
This is the algebraic basis for solving symmetry subproblems and reconstructing
their partners. At boundary wavevectors, fractional
translations can produce a projective multiplication law,
Blaze matches the representation to that factor system. Glide sectors cannot
in general be assigned the ordinary reflection labels valid at \Gamma.
Complex characters remain complex where required.
Splitting the space does not determine how many of the lowest bands lie in each
sector. Blaze retains conservative reference prefixes and offers adaptive
occupancy with explicit guards and cutoff-cluster checks. Partner reconstruction
preserves physical multiplicity; equal frequencies are not deduplicated into
one mode. The scalar zero-frequency kernel at \Gamma has one owner.
Returned modes receive fresh residual and mass-orthogonality checks in the
original finite pencil. Comparing degenerate modes uses their subspace, since
individual basis vectors may rotate within a cluster. A small residual alone
does not establish that the requested lowest bands are complete.
The eigensolver's stopping tolerance and these independent certificate
thresholds have different normalizations; a configured 1e-14 tolerance is not
a claim that every reported physical residual is below 1e-14.
For fixed active sector widths m_s and N spatial coefficients, the main
algebraic opportunities are
These are cost scalings, not measured speedup factors. Full-grid FFT work remains
roughly linear in the total number of columns. Sector guards, extra iterations,
projection and initialization can increase that total. Blaze therefore measures
the Gram/Ritz kernels, the shared iteration engine and the complete independent
sector control separately. A faster block operation can sit inside a slower
solver architecture.
PT real arithmetic
When inversion and time reversal combine into a qualified antiunitary symmetry
J with J^2=I, the fixed subspace Ju=u admits real coordinates. For the
supported inversion gauge, these are real Fourier coordinates. An origin
shift changes the gauge; it does not authorize deleting imaginary parts from a
spatial field. A global field phase can be absorbed in the real gauge of this
isolated scalar problem without changing its spectrum. Translated antiunitaries
can instead square to -I, which does
not permit this packing.
Blaze keeps f64 scalar precision while replacing eligible complex vector,
Gram and Ritz operations with real ones. Separate TM and tensor-TE kernels act
directly on that representation. MPB also provides a real-Fourier inversion
symmetry build; that is useful context, not a prediction of Blaze's
speedup.
Eligible persistent vectors need roughly half the scalar storage, with padding
and other allocations still present. Process RSS is measured separately. A
sector can compose with PT only if its projector preserves the qualified real
subspace. Complex rotational sectors retain complex coordinates where needed.
Blaze still exports the physical complex field.
Storage reduction and reduced operator work
An orbit basis S stores independent coefficients and reconstructs the full
field. The corresponding reduced pencil is
If each application expands to the full grid, this saves persistent storage but
still performs full-grid FFT work. Blaze reports that mode separately from its
genuine reduced TM and TE mirror kernels. Those kernels reduce transform work
only for the supported mirror, grid and material combinations; reconstructed
actions are checked against the full operator.
The optional reciprocal-metric support selects a different Galerkin pencil.
A metric ball can be closed under rotations that fail on a rectangle. Its sector
control is the unrestricted problem on the same support. A passing projected
residual does not prove convergence to the rectangular problem or the continuum;
resolution and material-sampling convergence remain separate checks.
The public metric-support workflow accepts f64 geometry-sampled material,
qualified PT, star/time-reversal reuse, target-metric seeds and coarse starts.
It keeps the supplied path order. A projected cache includes the exact support
identity and a projected certificate; it cannot authorize reuse on the original
rectangle. Group sectors retain complex coefficients. At a trivial little group,
or after sector rejection, the unrestricted support can use qualified PT.
Symmetry-compatible material averages
Select dielectric.smoothing = "voronoi" to average over the sampling lattice's
Wigner–Seitz cells. For a disk D and a cell V_i, its exact area fraction is
f_i=|D\cap V_i|/|V_i|. Blaze computes both
Circle/polygon boundary integrals supply the area and the averaged interface
normal. The existing TE interface rule then forms, in the grad-div convention,
On an equal-resolution triangular grid, these cells and normals rotate with C6.
Area conservation and scalar/tensor covariance are checked independently of the
solver. This changes the sampled material explicitly; the existing analytic
smoother retains its original behavior and its observable C6 failures.
Voronoi smoothing currently requires nonoverlapping periodic disks and
node-centered sampling. Refining the Fourier cutoff and the material grid remain
separate accuracy requirements.
Geometry continuation and automatic selection
bands.symmetry.continuation = "previous_geometry" carries the latest certified
spectrum at each compatible k point into the next geometry. "first_point"
limits this to the first executed point. Different sampled materials provide
initial directions after target-mass rank extraction and Ritz preparation.
Only an identical sampled operator and support, followed by a fresh certificate,
can skip a solve. Failed prepared initializers retry the ordinary path, and the
iteration ledger retains discarded work.
max_continuation_bytes bounds stored numerical payload across native workers.
Workers own private caches and deterministic geometry chains; job IDs and output
order remain stable. Explicit thread counts are respected. With automatic worker
counts, continuation chains retain multiple geometries where possible. Browser
calculation objects retain the same serial context between runJob calls.
Output arrays, FFT plans and library scratch have separate memory costs.
bands.symmetry.policy = "auto" selects among measured options and records its
model version, reasons, resolved configuration and runtime fallbacks. Numerical
qualification still governs every selected optimization. Automatic mode does
not change the material, Fourier support or precision. It is the default for band
calculations without mechanism keys; writing a mechanism key selects the manual
policy for explicit experiments, and external dielectric input always runs manually.
The residual-pt-v1 policy attempts PT on native f64 square/triangular FFT grids
with equal dimensions 16–128 and 8–16 bands when bands stop on a relative residual
between 1e-8 and 1e-6 (the default stopping rule), provided the objects are
symmetric under inversion about the cell origin. It caches repeated requested
k points. Under eigenvalue-change stopping it keeps the earlier calibration: grids
31–65 at tolerance at most 1e-13, and for triangular metric balls a cutoff with
0.40 \le R/N \le 0.46, with R measured in units of 2\pi/a. Outside the
envelope the original complex solve remains available. A failed PT attempt disables
further automatic PT retries for that geometry. Calibration used centered circular
rods; numerical qualification is still required for other motifs. These bounds are
an empirical policy, not a theorem about performance.
Qualification with eigenvalue-change stopping at 1e-6 found that PT attempts
consistently failed the strict physical certificate and incurred a second solve,
so that rule keeps complex arithmetic at looser tolerances. Residual stopping
certifies each solve directly. Close frequencies alone did not establish accurate
fields. The optional [bands.accuracy] contract
now checks every final output, including the ordinary fallback: convergence,
absolute-or-relative residuals and B-orthogonality. See API & TOML
for its limits, Gamma behavior and execution summaries.
The current public controls do not justify automatic geometry continuation:
unconditional full-path seeds regressed slightly, and first-point seeds could
trigger costly PT fallback. Qualification establishes correctness, not a timing
gain. Coarse starts and sectors likewise need their own matched workload evidence.
The implementation also retains research APIs for snapshot enrichment, projected
geometry-response solves, response selection rules, precision experiments and
bounded sector workers. Their preparation and failed work count toward cost.
Results from separate experiments are never multiplied into a combined speedup.
Configuring an experiment
The Workbench, native command and Python interface share the public
configuration contract. Native band calculations use the measured policy by default;
written out with an accuracy contract it reads:
[bands.symmetry]
policy = "auto"

[bands.accuracy]
max_relative_residual = 1e-5
max_absolute_residual = 1e-7
max_orthogonality_defect = 1e-8
Setting an eigenvalue-change tolerance here would leave the residual-stopping
envelope for the narrower eigenvalue-change calibration. The following blocks instead
illustrate an explicit PT experiment:
[eigensolver]
precision = "f64"
tolerance = 1e-14
max_iterations = 500

[bands.symmetry]
arithmetic = "pt_real"
k_reuse = "off"
k_traversal = "given"
Begin with a matching spatial_complex control. To test sectors, select a
qualified plane group and sector policy separately. To test a coarse start, add
an explicit coarse resolution and seed-field budget. Keep the fine grid,
material, bands, tolerances and output contract fixed. Configuration validation
and runtime qualification are both part of eligibility.
The replacement notes and benchmark record explain the
current positive results, regressions, timing exclusions and implementation
boundaries. No reported FFT element count or modeled payload is a measurement
of physical DRAM bandwidth or energy.
H. Wondratschek, Matrices, mappings and crystallographic symmetry, IUCr teaching pamphlet.
J. Fang, X. Gao and A. Zhou, A Symmetry-based Decomposition Approach to Eigenvalue Problems: Formulation, Discretization, and Implementation (2012). A general decomposition reference; its discretizations and measured applications differ from Blaze.
MIT Photonic Bands, Installation documentation, inversion-symmetry configuration.

title: Symmetry replacement notes
description: What changed in Blaze's symmetry solver, what validation corrected, and where the measured reductions help or regress.

headings.text: Negative results govern the automatic policy
Earlier mechanism measurements and their scope

text:
Symmetry replacement notes
Blaze's symmetry redesign replaces group-name heuristics and independent
full-grid sector experiments with exact affine actions and qualification of the
finite Maxwell pencil. This page records the replacement, including unsuccessful
optimizations. The Symmetries theory page develops the mathematics;
the Roadmap places the module in the wider project.
Starting point
The pinned starting revision is f4730cc4f119c6680c568bb5e998f86c3b0b19ad.
The older projector implementation had already been removed from production.
Its archived code combined array reflections, parity projectors and independent
sector solves. Projected vectors still occupied the full FFT grid, while each
sector duplicated initialization, guards and workspaces. The surviving band
driver used continuation and a closing-Γ shortcut, without general qualified
k-star reuse.
The problem was therefore broader than adding more group labels. A valid
continuum operation may fail on a sampled material, smoothed tensor or finite
Fourier support. A valid projector may save storage without reducing FFT work.
Several smaller solves can cost more than one unrestricted solve.
What changed
| Area | Replacement |
|---|---|
| Coordinates | Explicit direct/reciprocal conventions; the hexagonal K corner is (2/3, 1/3) for Blaze's 60-degree direct basis |
| Crystal actions | Integer lattice automorphisms, rational translations and origins, exact closure and lattice carries for all 17 plane groups |
| Bloch fields | Reciprocal folding and translation phases; axial TE reflection signs; explicit unitary and antiunitary actions |
| Eligibility | Separate metric, material/tensor, grid, support and operator qualification |
| Reuse | Identical-request reuse, qualified unitary/time-reversal stars, optional traversal and restored output order |
| Seeds | Lossless identity-aware caches; rank extraction and Ritz preparation in the target mass metric |
| Band coverage | Conservative references, adaptive sector occupancy and guards, cluster checks, complete partners and one Γ-kernel owner |
| PT | Qualified real Fourier coordinates in f64, with real vector/Gram/Ritz and direct TM/TE kernels |
| Reduced work | Orbit storage distinguished from genuine reduced mirror kernels and their transform dimensions |
| Galerkin support | Explicit reciprocal-metric support with its own unrestricted control, convergence and coverage checks |
| Research tracks | Geometry enrichment/response, response selection rules, coarse starts, precision, owned workers, bounded sweep scheduling and portable/WASM execution |
These are implementation changes and required failure controls. The table does
not assert that every listed mistake occurred in the pinned baseline.
The K correction changes the physical path, so it receives a corrected baseline
and is never counted as an optimization speedup.
Public parameter sweeps
The public runner now carries bounded certified continuation across full paths
and changing geometries, with private worker caches and deterministic geometry
chains. Original job IDs, output order and requested physical fields are
preserved. bands.symmetry.policy = "auto" adds a measured, versioned native
policy. It was opt-in for these measurements; with residual stopping it later became
the default (see API & TOML).
These complete CLI measurements use six unique radius/contrast combinations,
held-out radii 0.175/0.215/0.255 and dielectric constants 6.5/13, native f64,
tolerance 1e-14 and four workers. The 64² cases request 16 bands on a 16-point
closed path. They compare the original rectangle workflow at 3990221 with
automatic PT plus certified identical-point reuse, including process startup,
planning and JSON output. Each row has nine admitted randomized pairs, matching
spectra and fresh certificate/output checks. Linux raw and Windows QPC clocks
agree. Host checks permit light use; they do not reserve the machine.
| Public rectangle sweep | Reference / automatic time | Total iterations | Median peak RSS |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Square TM, 64² | 2.25× [2.23, 2.28] | 1790 → 1524 | 185.2 → 101.8 MiB |
| Square TE, 64² | 2.05× [2.03, 2.06] | 3600 → 3101 | 192.3 → 102.7 MiB |
| Triangular TM, 64² | 2.43× [2.40, 2.46] | 1915 → 1346 | 183.0 → 101.1 MiB |
| Triangular TE, 64² | 2.09× [2.07, 2.11] | 3758 → 3056 | 189.7 → 102.5 MiB |
The intervals are paired bootstrap 95% intervals for reference/candidate time.
Full complex field output was separately requested at 32², eight bands and ten
path points: square TE reached 1.52×, triangular TE 1.54×. The smaller
32² calibration sweeps with two workers reached about 1.45–1.54× for both
polarizations. These are fixture-specific gains, not multiplied microbenchmarks
or a guarantee for arbitrary motifs, paths, outputs or worker counts.
For the separately chosen triangular Voronoi material and metric support,
automatic PT plus identical-point reuse reaches 1.64× TM and 1.54× TE
at 64², 16 bands, cutoff R=28 and four workers. The reference uses exactly the
same material and support with complex Fourier arithmetic. At 32²/R=14, full
TE field output gives 1.22×. These comparisons do not count a smaller
Fourier support as an unchanged-physics speedup.
The public workflow data identifies each
comparison, revision, admitted/excluded blocks, time interval, iterations and
RSS. The repository report is benchmarks/symmetry/public-sweep-completion.md.
Negative results govern the automatic policy
Full-path geometry seeds were about 5% slower than matched controls. First-point
TM seeds triggered five rejected PT attempts and required ordinary fallback,
taking about 2.80 times the control time. First-point TE reduced iterations
slightly but did not produce a useful time saving. The triangular sector plus
coarse/geometry combination also regressed, despite matching spectra: the
held-out four-worker full-field case took 40% more time, with total iterations
increasing from 1904 to 5098 (including 376 coarse iterations). Along
these high-symmetry path segments, complex group sectors take precedence; merely
requesting PT does not mean PT executed inside those complex sectors.
Automatic selection therefore keeps geometry continuation, coarse starts and
sectors off in its calibrated native envelope. They remain available explicitly.
Each decision reports reasons and numerical fallbacks. A correctness certificate
does not establish profitability. Packed columns halve scalar storage, but output
and scratch costs remain; RSS and FFT counters are not DRAM-bandwidth measurements.
Triangular TE qualification
Voronoi-cell material averaging restores C6 covariance of the sampled scalar
and inverse-tensor data for the supported disks. Complete small-matrix defects
are around floating-point roundoff; the original analytic smoother's defects
remain visible. Independent source/support checks still authorize each action.
The new convergence series varies material sampling and cutoff independently.
At Gamma, the maximum scaled frequency difference from a separately certified
same-grid full rectangle decreases from 0.00702 at 33²/R=14 to 0.00214 at
65²/R=28 and 0.00118 at 129²/R=56. It still misses the declared 0.001 target.
A separate edge-cutoff follow-up at 129²/R=64 passes that target at Gamma and K,
with differences 0.000583 and 0.000600 and guarded-subspace sine errors below
0.00181. This is finite-reference agreement, not a continuum error bound.
At the generic point, six corrective iterations at the original tolerance
bring the independent reference through its residual gate. The R=64 comparison
then has scaled frequency error 0.000561 and guarded-subspace sine 0.00232.
All three points pass the stated finite-reference targets. Sampling changes
also decrease along the refinement sequence; this does not establish a continuum
error bound. All initial failures and unsuccessful over-tight stopping
experiments remain in the record.
Production interface hardening
The public interface now has an optional final [bands.accuracy] gate and a
concise execution summary. The summary separates requested mechanisms, retained
solves, reused points, declined optimizations and accuracy acceptance. The gate
checks convergence, an absolute-or-relative residual bound for every mode and
B-orthogonality, including ordinary fallbacks. Omission preserves the earlier
numerical defaults. The API guide includes a complete example
and recommended, advanced and experimental option labels.
A targeted nine-condition qualification at the ordinary 1e-6 stopping
tolerance exposed a profitability gap in automatic policy v2. No condition
retained PT output. In the symmetric rectangular studies, a rejected PT attempt
added about 14–18% more iterations before returning the ordinary result. The
loose metric-support study failed both paths' existing acceptance checks.
Close frequencies did not establish sufficiently accurate eigenvectors.
public-sweep-v3 therefore skips PT above stopping tolerance 1e-13. A separate
control collection retains one warmup and six admitted randomized pairs for
each of the same nine conditions. All eight completed rectangular studies have
bit-for-bit identical manual/automatic arrays and iteration counts, with time
ratios 0.981–1.020, within the declared 5% practical band. The metric condition
still rejects both paths with equal failed work. These results remove a default
regression; they do not claim default-tolerance acceleration or improved field
accuracy. The tight-tolerance speedups above retain their original scope.
The ordinary-setting record includes
both policy versions and their limitations.
The optional Python align_modes helper creates a separate reference-aligned
visualization basis within complete degenerate clusters. It requires a common
physical coordinate convention, positive mass weights for TM, compatible spans
and an upper guard band. Original fields, ordering and certificates are preserved.
Approximate degeneracy does not confer a fresh eigenpair certificate on a rotated
visualization frame.
Release checks now include the existing final Python/WASM continuation cases
and complete worker profiling. A focused pull-request gate reuses the numerical,
fallback, cache, field and cancellation tests. Native Linux and Windows checks
have been executed locally. The complete hosted wheel matrix has not been run
for this local branch; macOS remains explicitly unvalidated because no runner
is available. No package or site publication is implied by local validation.
The focused checks also corrected a stale configuration test that still rejected
newly supported metric PT/reuse, and a summary-only double count of a failed
metric point whose partial fields had already been emitted. The underlying
solver-attempt ledger remained correct. Archived early summaries are preserved;
the current report counts each final point ledger once.
Earlier mechanism measurements and their scope
The replacement measurements use frozen executables and inputs, randomized
paired runs, independent Linux raw and Windows QPC clocks, and numerical checks
on every execution. Profiles run separately. The desktop analysis retains whole
pairs using host-load measurements alone, requires at least 12 of 20 measured
pairs, and shows the unfiltered result as a sensitivity check. A numerical
failure cannot be removed by the timing filter.
The times cover each benchmark's declared internal solver or interface boundary;
separate process windows provide clock and load checks. Browser loading time is
outside these comparisons.
The ratios below are reference time / candidate time. Values above one mean
a faster candidate. They describe specific experiments on an i9-13900K desktop
under WSL2, not a general performance guarantee. The
machine-readable benchmark record carries the
comparison identities, intervals, both timing estimates, memory measurements
and excluded results.
The earlier 263 declared mechanism comparisons are addressed: 214 have usable timing estimates,
13 fail accuracy or requested-path checks, nine retain excluded timing, and
27 are diagnostic-only profiled comparisons. One of the failed comparisons is
also instrumented; none of the instrumented runs supplies a primary speed claim.
| Fixed workload and change | Time ratio | What explains or limits it |
|---|---:|---|
| 65², 24-band TE path: complex → PT, strict tolerance | 1.80× | Iterations 312 → 309; median RSS 83.6 → 38.9 MiB. Most of the gain comes from cheaper representation and algebra |
| Eight equivalent points, 31² TE: unrestricted → PT plus star reuse | 7.74× | Seven solves are reconstructed; isolated gains do not multiply |
| Eight equivalent points, 31² TM: unrestricted → PT plus star reuse | 4.24× | The same solve elimination has a different payoff for TM |
| Γ, 65², 24-band TE: unrestricted → PT plus sectors | 0.82× | About 23% more time despite lower RSS; PT alone reaches 1.81× on this workload |
| 65², 16-band TM mirror sweep: response → symmetry-selected response | 1.46× | Skipping forbidden response blocks helps at this scale |
| 31², 8-band TM radius sweep: copied seed → response predictor | 0.66× | Outer iterations 89 → 101, plus 768 inner response iterations |
| Γ, 65², 16-band TM: cold → public coarse initializer | 1.13× | Fine iterations 17 → 11; coarse work brings the total to 28; processed FFT elements fall by about 10% |
| 31², 8-band TE at generic k: f64 → f32 seed and f64 finish | 1.10–1.12× | Two seed budgets pass the final accuracy checks; this is not a pure-f32 result |
| 65², 16-band TM repeated parameter jobs: given order → routed order | 2.39× | Solves 10 → 5 and iterations 391 → 144, with the same cache capacity and requested output |
| 31², 8-band TE square sectors: one owned worker → four | 2.19× | Median RSS 11.8 → 29.4 MiB; this controls scheduling, not sectors versus unrestricted solving |
The full matrix also contains regressions and inconclusive differences.
Projective sectors help some larger glide cases, while several hexagonal TM
cases regress. Most tested public TE coarse starts are slower, including a
small PT case that takes about 52% more time. Pure f32 can produce close
frequencies while failing residual or orthogonality requirements; those cases
have no accepted speed claim. Dispatch and memory-admission refactors have
separate controls and show no material runtime regression in these tests.
Some f64 source controls also fail their fresh residual gate; successful
candidates in those comparisons establish a convergence difference, not a
timing gain. Accurate output obtained through fallback is not credited as a
successful execution of an explicitly requested optimization.
These findings support selective, explicitly qualified options. They do not
justify enabling every reduction together. An iteration on a coarse grid is
not equal in cost to one on a fine grid. RSS measures resident process memory;
FFT element counts and modeled payloads do not measure DRAM bandwidth or energy.
The earlier corrected support-convergence study also reproduces exactly. All 184
uninstrumented conditions pass their projected solver checks, but only 33 meet
the separate approximation target against the full rectangle, and all 33 are
TM. Smaller support changes the finite pencil; it is not automatically an
accurate replacement or a symmetry speedup.
Corrections retained in the record
Degenerate subspaces. The first metric-support comparison guarded clusters
only in the reference spectrum. In 41 records it cut a candidate cluster. The
corrected comparison closes the prefix in both spectra. Original records and
their replacements remain identifiable.
Invalid memory experiment. An initial workspace-admission comparison used
identical baseline and candidate executables. That experiment is invalid.
Separately isolated builds with distinct verified hashes replace it; its
original measurements are preserved as an erratum.
PT-sector leakage. A warm TE return amplified roundoff beyond the existing
leakage limit. Final sector projection before coordinate Ritz refinement fixes
the path and records the correction. The acceptance tolerance was unchanged.
On the portable backend, a failed PT continuation can fall back to certified
spatial arithmetic, with discarded work included in the total.
Public profile publication. Automatic scoped-worker completion could
precede publication from thread-local destructors, omitting entire workers from
the exported profile while numerical results were complete. Explicitly joining
every worker before the terminal event fixes the race. Replacement profiles
require their iteration counter to equal the independent result ledger. Initial
incomplete profiles are retained as invalid work evidence; uninstrumented
primary timings are separate.
Profiling semantics. Nested inclusive times cannot be added into a cost
breakdown. The profiler now distinguishes inclusive/exclusive timing and work
counters. Frozen trial-matrix tests and the actual shared iteration engine are
separate experiments. Instrumented timings do not become unprofiled speed claims.
Contended benchmarks and clocks. Earlier measurements overlapped other
workloads and are provisional. During remeasurement, the WSL adjusted timer was
found to run about 1.1 times the agreeing Linux raw and Windows QPC clocks. The
new evidence keeps raw samples, independent clock witnesses and a separate
normalization. Timing exclusions preserve correctness evidence and remain
visible; a contaminated or numerically failed experiment is not reported as a
win.
Supported boundaries
The rectangular f64 workflow supports qualified reuse, traversal, seeds,
ordinary/projective sectors, partner reconstruction, Fourier/PT coordinates,
selected orbit/reduced-mirror paths and an optional first-point coarse start.
Composition still depends on the material, finite support and representation.
An unsupported real sector keeps complex coordinates where the workflow permits
it; invalid configuration combinations produce an error.
The public reciprocal-metric support accepts f64 geometry sampling, PT,
star/time-reversal reuse, coarse starts and bounded cross-geometry continuation.
It retains supplied path order. Complex group sectors and the unrestricted PT
path are selected separately; packing a general complex irrep as real is not
claimed. Voronoi-cell smoothing supplies a separately selected C6-compatible
material for nonoverlapping periodic disks. Existing analytic smoothing keeps
its original values and observable qualification failures.
No GPU backend or general magnetic corepresentation implementation is claimed.
Later research mechanisms have Rust APIs and frozen experiments. Response and precision experiments remain explicit research choices. Certified
continuation now runs through native/Python sweeps and serial browser calculation
objects; automatic policy promotion additionally requires public timing evidence.
Native/portable tests, actual WASM execution, Python/CLI checks and three-browser
checks cover the shared public workflows. Legacy parent/candidate comparisons
also check full numerical outputs. Independent physical audits distinguish
missing material-preview information from an actually verified field.
The implementation and experiment ledger is maintained in
benchmarks/symmetry/implementation-status.md; the repository's Markdown
replacement record is benchmarks/symmetry/replacement-changelog.md.

title: Master’s Thesis
description: Why twisted photonic crystals need a two-scale theory, how the second edition tests it, and why that work led to Blaze2D.

headings.text: From Maxwell to a slow envelope
Matching every state in a declared domain
What remains unresolved at strong coupling
Does a smaller twist make flatter bands?

text:
Master’s thesis · TU Dortmund · Second edition, September 2026
Photonic moiré crystals
How a two-scale description of twisted crystals led to Blaze2D.
A photonic crystal controls light through a repeating pattern of dielectric material.
Twist two such patterns against each other and their local alignment changes slowly
across space. That extra structure can reshape the optical bands, reduce propagation
speeds and confine modes. The question behind this thesis was how to calculate those
effects directly from Maxwell’s equations without resolving every microscopic cell
of a large twisted structure.
The answer developed in Photonic Band Theory of Moire Crystals: A Two-Scale Approach
is an envelope theory built from local Bloch modes. It replaces one large calculation
with many small crystal calculations and a separate problem for the slow modulation.
Blaze2D was built to supply those local calculations, including the operator data
needed to connect them.
This page follows the revised derivation and results in the second edition. Read the full thesis.
Why direct calculations become expensive
A periodic band solver needs a repeating cell. A generic twist has no exact repeating
bilayer cell. Special, commensurate angles do, but those cells grow rapidly as the angle
shrinks. At a fixed microscopic resolution, the number of grid points grows roughly
as \theta^{-2}. Memory, factorization and repeated eigensolves then become the bottleneck.
This was concrete in the revised square-bilayer study. The FDFD reference at 2.01^\circ
used about 3.3 million unknowns and took 3,221 seconds. The next cell at 1.01^\circ
would need about 13 million unknowns and did not fit in the workstation’s memory.
An angle sweep therefore needed a description whose grid follows the slow physics.
Two scales from one twist
Each monolayer has a lattice spacing a. Their changing alignment introduces the much
larger moiré period L. For identical lattices near alignment,
Here the small-angle approximation uses radians. A 2^\circ twist gives L\approx29a.
The dots below show the microscopic scale; the white arrows and cell show the slow
stacking pattern. Change the angle to see the two scales separate. The enlarged
monolayer cells keep their size while the moiré cell changes.
The moiré cell describes a repeating pattern of local alignment. It is not generally
an exact supercell of all the dielectric objects. That distinction is what lets the
theory address angles at which a periodic full-structure calculation is unavailable.
At large twists the geometric construction still works, but the two scales are no
longer well separated and the small-angle theory loses its basis.
From Maxwell to a slow envelope
For a lossless, non-magnetic medium with scalar permittivity \varepsilon(x,y), the
strictly two-dimensional problem separates into two polarizations:
Locally, a small-angle bilayer resembles an ordinary periodic crystal with a relative
shift between its two constituents. This shift is the registry, \boldsymbol\delta.
Moving through the moiré pattern changes the registry slowly, so the local Bloch modes
can serve as a basis for the full field:
The u_n resolve the fast crystal oscillations near a chosen carrier momentum
\mathbf k_0. The amplitudes f_n describe the slow envelope. Only a selected group
of bands, P, is retained. Its separation from the other bands matters: a small twist
alone cannot make a poorly isolated band group into a valid reduced model.
What the effective Hamiltonian contains
Projecting Maxwell’s operator onto these local modes and expanding through second
order in \eta gives the following compact TE form:
It acts on the envelope via \mathcal H_{\mathrm{eff}}f=\lambda f, with the dimensionless
\lambda=(\omega a/c)^2. Repeated spatial indices are summed.
Local band energies \Lambda describe how the spectrum changes with registry.
Velocity and inverse mass describe the local band slopes and curvatures. The mass includes virtual coupling to bands outside P through Löwdin downfolding.
Covariant momentum \Pi_i=-i\mathcal D_i includes the Berry connection, which tracks how the retained Bloch basis changes from one registry to another.
Remainder operators contain the remaining scalar and derivative terms, including the Born-Huang contribution from the basis changing into the discarded band space.
These coefficients are tabulated on the registry domain for a fixed material and band
choice, then reused at different twists. For TM, transforming the field with
\widetilde E_z=\varepsilon^{1/2}E_z makes the eigenproblem Hermitian in the ordinary
inner product. Derivatives of the factor \rho=\varepsilon^{-1/2} then contribute
additional terms. The complete expressions and definitions are collected in these
two annotated posters.
Why this required Blaze2D
The reduced problem is smaller, but assembling it needs more than band frequencies.
Each registry point requires Bloch eigenvectors, velocity and mass matrix elements,
momentum and registry derivatives, and couplings between retained and remote bands.
Keeping four bands can require solving sixteen or more, repeated at thousands of
slightly different crystal configurations.
MPB provided a valuable reference. Its Python interface
also exposes fields, raw eigenvectors and group velocities. The missing part for this
thesis was direct access to the specific projected operators and interband couplings
needed by the envelope construction. Those quantities were not available as the
operator dataset the pipeline required. Extracting them, with consistent normalization
and gauge conventions across a registry sweep, was a separate problem from computing
a band diagram.
Blaze2D combines that access with a Rust plane-wave solver designed for repeated local
solves. Iterative eigensolves, warm starts, mixed precision and parallel parameter
studies address throughput; explicit Bloch and operator outputs address the data
bottleneck. Blaze supplies the microscopic inputs. The MSL research pipeline
assembles and solves the moiré envelope problem from them.
Reading the results
The following sections present results from the thesis and assume some familiarity
with photonic bands and effective models. For a visual overview of the operator
data provided by Blaze, jump to What the operator data reveal.
What the second edition establishes
The central test is whether the small envelope problem reproduces the full crystal’s
frequencies. EA labels the envelope approximation, assembled by MSL from Blaze’s
local Bloch data. The independent references solve Maxwell’s equations on the full
structure: PWE uses plane waves; FDFD uses a spatial grid. MPB adds a check
for the square bilayer. Every comparison uses the same dielectric and declared band domain.
Eigenvalues determine the crystal’s allowed frequencies. Similar-looking bands can
hide missing, extra or misplaced modes. Matching every state in a range chosen
in advance tests both the frequencies and their count. Agreement near the reference’s
own numerical error shows how much the small model preserves. Frequency differences
below use f=\omega a/(2\pi c).
Convergence under controlled conditions
A frame is the set of local Bloch field patterns used to build the envelope
solution. Recall how the blue and orange dots change their local alignment across
the explorer’s white cell. That change in registry also changes the local modes.
A frozen frame reuses the modes from one registry and carrier momentum everywhere. The envelope can vary, but its microscopic field patterns stay fixed.
A registry-adapted frame recalculates those patterns as the local alignment changes. The envelope is built on modes that follow the crystal underneath it.
The first plot asks whether a smaller twist makes the prediction more accurate.
On this smooth, weakly coupled crystal, adaptation lowers the error about fifteenfold.
At fixed material, however, both models reach an error floor: the registry potential
becomes stronger relative to the slow kinetic energy as the angle shrinks.
A controlled test reduces the second-layer amplitude as a_2\propto\eta^2, keeping
that balance fixed. Its adapted model converges approximately as \eta^{3.8}
and reaches agreement with both full-Maxwell references of about
8\times10^{-7} in frequency. This rate belongs to that scaled family.
Matching every state in a declared domain
A frame also depends on momentum, which sets the wave’s direction and wavelength.
The “exact frames” below use a Bloch solution at each retained momentum, summing beyond
the low-order expansion. This separate weak-coupling test uses modes of the
registry-averaged crystal.
At 0.607^\circ, a supercell contains 8,911 microscopic cells. The chosen domain
covers states near one minimum of the local band, called a valley. The exact-frame
model matches all 51 states in that domain, with frequency differences of
4.7\times10^{-8} to 8.1\times10^{-8}. These are comparable to the measured
numerical error of the full-Maxwell reference.
Bands outside the retained set also influence how its modes propagate. The second-order
Löwdin correction includes this influence and recovers two to three orders of
accuracy on the affected states. Feshbach downfolding treats the same coupling
without that second-order truncation. Exact momentum-dependent frames improve it
further. The discarded bands contribute corrections, while the envelope state set
stays fixed.
What remains unresolved at strong coupling
The square rod bilayer is harder: its changing registry creates deep wells that
confine the envelopes. The revised model brings the lowest frequency close to the
full-wave references and reaches 0.50^\circ, where the full calculation did not
fit in memory. Higher in the spectrum, however, symmetry should make groups of four
modes share a frequency. The model splits these groups incorrectly. Its adapted
basis still needs a consistent phase and mixing convention, or gauge, that
respects the crystal’s symmetry.
What the operator data reveal
Figure 61 collects the local band data and Hamiltonian coefficients for a honeycomb TM crystal. Its retained
Dirac pair consists of two bands that meet at a cone-shaped crossing when aligned.
Each sheet maps a different quantity over the same local alignments, like moving
around the explorer’s white cell.
Read from the bottom up
Local spectrum. Above the crystal sit the two band energies and their gap. Their variation supplies the landscape the envelope moves through.
Propagation. The velocity and kinetic mass describe the slopes and curvatures of the local bands, including the influence of remote bands.
Changing modes. The Berry fields track changes within the retained pair. The Born-Huang term at the top records how its basis changes into discarded bands.
The same registry data can be mapped onto different moiré cell sizes. Changing the twist changes that spatial scale, as in the explorer above.
The maps below unpack the stack’s geometric part. The upper row shows the local gap
and two measures of how strongly the retained basis changes into other bands.
Bright lines mark the strongest changes.
A computed mode has an arbitrary phase; a nearly degenerate pair can also be mixed.
A gauge fixes these choices between neighbouring registries. The two Berry-connection
maps show how inconsistent choices can dominate the apparent variation. The Berry
curvature at bottom right is independent of that choice.
Does a smaller twist make flatter bands?
Flat bands and magic angles are of particular interest in physics. A study of band
flattening was therefore a natural application of the thesis’s effective model.
A moiré band traces an envelope mode’s frequency as its momentum changes. Its slope
sets the wave packet’s propagation speed, so flat bands are candidates for slow light.
The bandwidth measures the frequency spread along the sampled momentum path.
The pipeline scanned 237 angles from 0.2^\circ to 10^\circ. Above 1.5^\circ,
the typical bandwidth follows roughly \theta^{1.6}. At smaller angles the fixed-grid
calculation plateaus. No magic angle was established: the shallow minimum does
not demonstrate a collapse to a flat band. Resolving that question would require
finer, angle-dependent grids and a direct check of the propagation velocity.
Blaze exposes the local modes and operator matrix elements so a smaller model can
be assembled, tested and understood term by term. The second edition establishes that approach in controlled
regimes. Strong-coupling symmetry and an extension to photonic slabs remain open.

title: Workbench
description: Choose a model, configure a study, run it, inspect results, and export.
text:
Workbench
The Workbench runs Blaze2D in your browser. It uses the same
configuration contract as Python, with an f64 backend. Automatic stopping resolves
to the relative eigenvalue change in the browser and to the relative residual for
native band calculations.
Choose a model. Open the Examples tab, inspect a calculation, and select Load example. Its geometry, task, settings, and sweeps fill the workspace together. You can also import a TOML file.
Configure a study. The Setup sidebar has Crystal and Calculation controls. Geometry shows the crystal; Study shows the reciprocal-space path and calculation plan. Choose bands or operators, sampling, sweep axes, and retained outputs in Calculation.
Run. Start the calculation and inspect its progress. Cancel stops the browser worker immediately. Completed jobs remain available.
Inspect. Results contains band plots, arrays, dimensions, and convergence information. Select a configuration or stencil sample to inspect its data.
Export. Download NPZ, JSON, NDJSON, or the selected run's original TOML. History stores recent runs on this device.
The Geometry preview repeats the crystal and marks one unit cell. Switch between
Geometry and Dielectric grid, or change the number of visible periods.
Fractional and Cartesian change how object centers are displayed and edited;
the saved configuration uses fractional coordinates, wrapped into the unit cell.
Split view opens a second editor group. Choose a tab in either group to place
geometry beside results, TOML beside the preview, or examples beside your study.
Drag the divider, or focus it and use the arrow keys, to adjust the widths. On
small screens the groups stack vertically. Setup shows or hides the controls.
TOML is an editor tab that shares its configuration with the visual controls.
Edits require Apply or Revert. An invalid or unapplied draft blocks
execution and structured editing. Normalize expands defaults, removes comments,
validates the result, and applies it. A completed result always keeps the
configuration used for that run. The live band's horizontal axis uses the complete
planned path, so arriving points do not rescale it.
In the browser the eigensolver stopping tolerance measures relative eigenvalue
changes. Band and operator results also contain fresh residuals and an orthogonality
defect. [bands.accuracy] enforces an explicit final band acceptance policy;
operators.fail_on_residual is the operator threshold. Results separately show
stopping convergence and accuracy acceptance. The execution summary identifies
the requested symmetry policy, methods actually retained, reused points and
fallback reasons. Expand provenance for the complete numerical ledger.
The browser preflights a 512 MiB execution budget. History uses a bounded local
cache; export important results before leaving. Use Python for larger studies,
external dielectric arrays, reference fields, or checkpointed runs.
See Examples in the Workbench and API & TOML for reusable calculations
and the coordinate and array conventions.
